title: Australia’s Women, Peace and Security bill comes due
author: Michelle Higelin
text: Gender & equality, explained.Observance of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women at UN headquarters in New York (Loey Felipe/UN Photo)Australia’s Women, Peace and Security bill comes dueA surge in defence spending is reshaping the region – Australia's peacebuilding agenda deserves the same ambition.Michelle Higelin 30 July 20264 min read|Australia’s Women, Peace and Security bill comes dueAustralia’s Women, Peace and Security bill comes dueOver the past month, the Australian government has signed a series of defence pacts with regional neighbours – from Narendra Modi’s visit to Sydney, cementing India as a partner in defence-industry growth, to the long-awaited Nakamal Agreement with Vanuatu and the Ocean of Pacific Alliance treaty with Fiji.At the same time, China has asserted its military prowess in the Pacific with the launch of a long-range ballistic missile, in a year that also marks 60 years since nuclear testing began in the region, with lasting health, environmental and cultural harm.Australia’s annual defence budget is set to grow to $53 billion over the next decade as the country confronts what Defence Minister Richard Marles describes as the most “threatening circumstances since the end of World War II (Opens in new window)”.Yet questions remain over whether more spending on defence brings Australia any closer to peace – and how it aligns with the country’s commitments to the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda.More than 25 years ago, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 1325, launching the WPS agenda, which places women’s leadership at the heart of peacebuilding alongside commitments to prevent conflict-related sexual violence, protect the most vulnerable and drive inclusive relief and recovery. More than 110 countries (Opens in new window) now have National Action Plans (NAPs) on WPS, and regional strategies, such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Regional Action Plan on WPS, are emerging.Yet the past five years have brought dramatic regression from peace, driven by anti-rights movements, rising conflict and expanding militarisation. For the 11th consecutive year, global military expenditure has grown, reaching almost US$2.9 trillion (Opens in new window).Choices about where money flows are choices about the vision underpinning regional security.The message from 60 civil society leaders across 18 countries who gathered in Brisbane in August 2025 for a Regional Convening on WPS (Opens in new window) hosted by the Australian WPS Coalition was clear: a move must be made from policy to implementation. The task ahead is to make the WPS agenda integral to the vision for a more secure Australia and region, matched by equivalent ambition in resourcing.Four priorities stand out.It starts with funding plans that already exist. National Action Plans are a genuine achievement, but they are underfunded and weakly institutionalised. Without dedicated budgets, strong monitoring and evaluation, and mechanisms to support women’s rights organisations, the agenda risks stagnating.As a leading regional donor, Australia should step up investment in women’s participation in peacebuilding, conflict resolution and humanitarian response, alongside the prevention of sexual and gender-based violence. Funding must also reach frontline women’s rights organisations as core, flexible, multi-year funding rather than short project grants. These groups deliver results on the ground yet carry a disproportionate burden in crises with the least secure funding.The climate–gender gap must also be closed. Climate change is not an adjacent concern but a defining peace and security challenge for the region, with extreme weather already intensifying displacement and gender-based violence. Australia’s first Nationally Determined Contribution – the plan to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change – was gender-blind (Opens in new window), while the second, released in September 2025, recognises the unequal gendered impacts of climate change but lacks measurable targets (Opens in new window).Closing the gap requires scaled-up investment in women-led climate justice initiatives and embedding climate across all four pillars of Australia’s WPS plan – participation, protection, prevention, and relief and recovery. With Australia’s Climate Minister Chris Bowen presiding over COP31 this year, there is an opportunity to ensure gender expertise is at the negotiating table rather than on the margins, and to resource Pacific and Indigenous women’s participation.A further priority is to invest in Indigenous feminist peacebuilding at home. As part of advancing its First Nations foreign policy, Australia can embed Indigenous feminist perspectives in its WPS framework, recognising over 65,000 years of community-based models of peace, care for Country and truth-telling. This means enabling resource exchange among Indigenous feminist peacebuilders across Australia, Asia and the Pacific, and supporting Indigenous women’s engagement in domestic, regional and global WPS agendas. This framing aligns the agenda with realities First Nations women have long identified.A priority must also be to make inclusion structural, not symbolic, matching calls across the region to move “beyond tokenism”. Representation quotas for Indigenous, youth, LGBTQIA+, refugee, diaspora women and people with disabilities mean little without resourcing for travel, interpretation, care responsibilities and accessibility. Engagement with LGBTQIA+ organisations is often inconsistent and at times unsafe, and disability inclusion is acknowledged in policy but limited in practice.Investing in the conditions for genuine participation of diverse women – and in young women’s emerging leadership – is critical to building shared decision-making power and sustaining the agenda over the longer term.Underlying all four priorities is a call to lift investment in the WPS agenda to at least 5% of current defence spending. This is essential to build a more secure region amid rising militarisation, climate shocks and backsliding on women’s rights. Choices about where money flows are choices about the vision underpinning regional security.For the Australian government, stepping up looks less like new declarations and pacts and more like paying for the ones already made – including those enshrined in its Second National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security.About the authorMichelle Higelin Michelle Higelin is the Executive Director of ActionAid Australia and Co-Chair of the Australian Civil Society Coalition on Women, Peace and Security.TopicsGender & equalityAustraliaDefence & securityClimate & environmentPacific IslandsThe Interpreter on Gender & equalityExplore The InterpreterAfghanistanAustralia must do more for Afghanistan28 July 2026Naomi BrooksGender & equalityGender is everywhere in Southeast Asian aid, but not where it counts6 July 2026Dyah (Prita) PritadrajatiPhilippinesSea Angels: The Philippines turned communication into a security tool15 June 2026Joy Dianne GumatayMore on Gender & equalityExplore Gender & equalityResearchMainstreamed but sidelined: Global funding for gender equalityPolicy Brief by Grace StanhopeConversationsWomen, security, power and policyLydia Khalil, Susannah Patton, Serena SasingianEvent HighlightsPacific Panel: Advancing women in business and leadershipPenny Wong, Jessica CollinsEvent ReplayWomen and foreign policy: Perspectives from the Lowy InstituteJennifer Hsu, Jessica Collins, Meg Keen + 1 other
